transcript:
This message comes from Capital One with the Capital One Saver card.
Earn unlimited 3% cash back on dining and entertainment.
Capital One.
What's in your wallet?
Terms apply.
Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
President Trump says the U.S. war with Iran is "effectively over."
He spoke yesterday after meeting Qatar's Prime Minister at the White House.
Trump may be paying attention to last week's midterm election results,
but NPR's Deepa Shivram says it's not clear what Trump's next actions might be.
So it's within the realm of possibility that Trump picks back up on military action.
If he isn't getting a deal that he wants, he said that the U.S. is still "locked and loaded" if needed.
At the same time, Trump has acknowledged that the war played a part in Republicans losing control of Congress,
saying he knows that high prices because of the war were a big issue for voters this year.
But he also continues to dig his heels in and say the war was necessary and he would do it over again.
NPR's Deepa Shivram reporting.
Shares in computer chip maker Nvidia dropped more than 4% in yesterday's trading.
That happened after the company announced it was launching an investigation involving its CEO.
He's admitted to a romantic relationship, but published reports suggest the woman may have been spying for China.
And PR's John Ruich reports.
Nvidia shares took a beating while the rest of the market bounced back after losses last week.
The company said on Sunday it's investigating CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
But for now, Huang is still in charge of the $4.3 trillion company that he co-founded more than 30 years ago.
The New York Times has reported that US intelligence agencies believed Huang was having an affair with a Chinese woman at a Singapore-based company that had bought Nvidia chips
and that she was recruited by China's top spy agency.
NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting.
John Ruich, NPR News.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is scheduled to speak next hour.
He's expected to criticize the impeachment articles filed against him yesterday in the House.
He's called the effort a sham.
The Supreme Court hears arguments today in a case that could undercut the ability of many federal regulatory agencies to fine businesses.
NPR's Nina Totenberg reports the cases involve violations of federal laws.
For decades, farmers have relied on a federal immigration program that allows them to temporarily employ migrant workers during crop season.
In addition to wages, farm owners must provide basic necessities such as housing, food and water.
In 2016, the U.S. Department of Labor fined Sun Valley and New Jersey Farm a half million dollars for unsanitary conditions, including providing unsafe drinking water and multiple other alleged defenses.
At the Supreme Court today, Sun Valley is disputing the charges and contends that imposing fines based on administrative proceedings but without a jury trial is unconstitutional.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The government will release its latest reports on inflation this morning, but it won't be a full report.
Officials cannot compare numbers from October last month to October last year.
That's because last year there was a six-week federal shutdown and October inflation prices were never officially collected.
Editors and publishers are being inundated with AI-generated submissions.
Some are turning to detection tools, and B.R.'s Windsor Johnston reports the tools don't always get it right.
The flood of suspected writing generated by AI means more work for editors.
Neil Clark is the publisher of the science fiction magazine Clark's World.
It's adding so much to our workload. I know that mine is increased by 25 to 30 percent.
AI detectors look for patterns in language.
Chris Callison-Burch is an artificial intelligence expert at the University of Pennsylvania.
Adverbs like notably or crucially at the beginning of sentences are often AI writing or things that are self-posed rhetorical questions.
But people use those word patterns, too, so human writing can get flagged as AI.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
The U.S. Postal Service says it will release new stamps next year honoring two athletic stars.
One features the late Pat Summit.
She led the Tennessee women's basketball team to eight championships.
The other stamp will honor baseball's Hall of Famer, the iconic Willie Mays.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.

That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Trump says U.S. war with Iran is effectively over, keeps military option open
Nvidia shares fall over 4% after probe into CEO Jensen Huang over alleged Chinese spy ties
Hegseth to speak next hour, expected to criticize House impeachment articles against him
Supreme Court hears arguments in Sun Valley farm case on federal agency fines without jury trial
Government to release partial October inflation report, as last year's shutdown left data uncollected
Editors overwhelmed by AI-generated submissions; detection tools often flag human writing
U.S. Postal Service to issue 2027 stamps honoring Pat Summitt and Willie Mays
